title: The Hedgerow
text:
Here is a practical guide to The Hedgerow in English, organized step by step.

---

 A Practical Guide to The Hedgerow

 Step 1: Understand What a Hedgerow Is
A hedgerow is a dense line of shrubs, bushes, and sometimes small trees planted closely together. It is used to mark boundaries, provide privacy, support wildlife, and protect soil and crops.

 Step 2: Choose the Right Location
- Select a boundary line, roadside, garden edge, or field margin.
- Make sure the area gets enough sunlight and has adequate soil drainage.
- Avoid placing it where it will block important views, drainage, or access routes.

 Step 3: Decide the Purpose
Before planting, clarify why you want the hedgerow:
- Privacy screen
- Windbreak
- Wildlife habitat
- Farm or property boundary
- Aesthetic landscaping

Your purpose will determine the plant species and planting density.

 Step 4: Select Suitable Plant Species
Choose plants that match your climate, soil, and maintenance capacity.
- Native species are best for wildlife and local conditions.
- Deciduous shrubs offer seasonal change.
- Evergreen shrubs provide year-round cover.
- Thorny species can improve security and shelter.

Common choices may include hawthorn, blackthorn, hazel, holly, dogwood, and field maple.

 Step 5: Prepare the Ground
- Clear weeds, grass, and debris along the planting line.
- Loosen the soil to help roots establish.
- Add compost or organic matter if the soil is poor.
- Mark the planting line with string or stakes.

 Step 6: Plant in the Right Season
- The best time is usually late autumn to early spring, when plants are dormant.
- Avoid planting during frost or very dry periods.
- Space plants according to species and purpose, often 30–60 cm apart for a dense hedge.

 Step 7: Plant Correctly
- Dig a hole wide enough for the roots.
- Place the plant at the same depth as it was in the pot or nursery bed.
- Backfill with soil and firm gently.
- Water well after planting.

 Step 8: Water and Mulch
- Water regularly during the first year, especially in dry weather.
- Apply mulch around the base to retain moisture and reduce weeds.
- Keep mulch away from direct contact with stems.

 Step 9: Protect Young Plants
- Use tree guards or fencing if animals may damage the hedge.
- Remove competing weeds around the base.
- Replace any failed plants promptly.

 Step 10: Prune and Maintain
- Prune lightly in the first few years to encourage dense growth.
- Trim hedges after nesting season if wildlife is present.
- Cut sides and tops according to the desired shape and height.
- Remove dead, diseased, or damaged wood.

 Step 11: Manage for Wildlife
- Let some sections grow taller and thicker.
- Allow flowers, berries, and seeds to develop.
- Leave leaf litter and dead wood where safe.
- Avoid pesticides and unnecessary cutting.

 Step 12: Review and Improve
- Check the hedgerow each season for gaps, disease, or storm damage.
- Replant bare spots.
- Adjust pruning and maintenance based on growth and purpose.
- Over time, a well-managed hedgerow becomes stronger, denser, and more valuable.

---

 Quick Tips
- Plant native species whenever possible.
- Plant early and water consistently.
- Prune at the right time of year.
- Think long-term: hedgerows improve with age.
- A good hedgerow supports both people and wildlife.

If you want, I can also make this into a one-page checklist, a school project version, or a British hedgerow-specific guide.

title: The Orchard in Winter
text:
The Orchard in Winter

 I. The Silent Gate

The gate stood half-open, its iron hinges furred with frost. No one had passed through it for days—perhaps weeks—and the snow had drifted undisturbed against its lower bars, forming a small white dune that sparkled faintly in the pale morning light. I pushed it gently, and it swung back with a low, mournful creak, as though reluctant to admit a visitor into so quiet a kingdom.

Beyond the gate, the orchard stretched in rows of bare, black trees, their branches etched against the grey sky like the veins of some enormous, sleeping leaf. The snow lay smooth between the rows, unmarked by any footprint, and the whole place seemed to hold its breath, waiting for something that might never come.

 II. The Architecture of Absence

In summer, these trees had been a green cathedral, their leaves whispering hymns to the sun. Now they were stripped to their essential selves—trunk, branch, twig—a geometry of endurance. Each tree stood alone, yet connected by the invisible threads of root and memory, their shadows long and blue upon the snow.

I walked slowly down the central aisle, my boots sinking with a soft, muffled crunch. The cold air smelled of bark and frozen earth, clean and austere, like the inside of an old wooden box. Above me, the branches interlaced, forming a lattice through which the winter light fell in fragments—not warm, not golden, but silver and spare, as if the sun itself had grown cautious.

 III. What the Snow Remembers

Here and there, a few withered apples still clung to the highest boughs, their skins wrinkled and dark, like the faces of old men who have seen too many seasons. The birds had not taken them; even the wasps had abandoned them. They hung there, small and forgotten, monuments to a sweetness that had once been.

I stopped beneath one such tree and looked up. The apple swayed slightly in a breeze I could not feel, and I thought of all the summers it had known—the bees, the rain, the heavy perfume of blossom, the laughter of children who had long since grown and gone. The snow remembers nothing, I thought. But the trees remember everything, and they keep their memories in rings of wood, hidden beneath the bark, waiting for someone to ask.

 IV. The Sound of Silence

There is a silence in the winter orchard that is not empty. It is full—full of the tiny sounds that summer drowns: the creak of a branch shifting under snow, the faint tick of a frozen twig, the distant call of a crow that seems to come from another world. I stood still and listened until I could hear my own heartbeat, slow and steady, keeping time with the pulse of the sleeping earth.

A single leaf, brown and curled, detached itself from a branch and drifted down, landing without a sound upon the snow. It was the only movement in the entire orchard, and I watched it as though it were a miracle—which, in a way, it was.

 V. The Promise Beneath

But even here, in the heart of winter, there was no despair. Beneath the snow, beneath the frozen ground, beneath the bark of every tree, life waited. I could feel it—a faint, persistent warmth, like a candle burning in a distant room. The orchard was not dead; it was dreaming.

I turned to leave, and as I did, I noticed a small bud on the lowest branch of the nearest tree—tight, brown, almost invisible, but there. It would be months before it opened, before the orchard would again be white with blossom and loud with bees. But it was there, a promise written in the smallest of letters, waiting to be read by the sun.

I walked back through the gate, and this time it closed behind me with a soft click, as though satisfied. The snow began to fall again, lightly, gently, covering my footprints. In an hour, there would be no sign that I had ever been there.

But I would remember. And somewhere in the quiet dark of the orchard, a single bud held its breath and dreamed of spring.

title: On Books and Firelight
text:
Here is a speech titled "On Books and Firelight."

---

On Books and Firelight

Good evening, everyone.

There is a particular kind of magic that happens when the modern world falls away and we are left with just two ancient companions: a book and a fire. I’d like to talk to you tonight about that magic.

We live in an age of relentless light. Screens glow at us from every angle, demanding our attention with notifications and headlines. The light is cold, blue, and urgent. It is the light of *now*. But the firelight is different. It is warm, amber, and slow. It is the light of *always*.

When you sit before a fire, you are participating in one of humanity’s oldest rituals. For millennia, our ancestors gathered around the flame. It was the center of the home, the source of heat, the protector against the dark. The fire did not just cook their food; it cooked their stories. It was around the fire that tales were told, legends were born, and history was passed down. The fire was the original library.

And then, we invented the book.

To bring a book into the circle of firelight is to unite two of the greatest technologies ever gifted to the human mind. The fire is the technology of *warmth*—it sustains the body and comforts the spirit. The book is the technology of *empathy*—it sustains the mind and expands the soul. When you open a book by the fire, you are not just reading. You are engaging in a conversation that spans centuries.

The fire is a living thing. It breathes, it shifts, it whispers. It casts dancing shadows on the walls that seem to animate the very words on the page. The flickering light demands that you slow down. You cannot skim a book by firelight. The light is too precious, too soft. It forces you to savor each sentence, to pause, to reflect. In that stillness, the boundary between the story and the reader begins to blur.

Who hasn’t felt it? You are reading a tale of a lonely journey, and the wind howls outside the window, making the fire sputter. You are reading of a great love, and the warmth of the embers on your face feels like a gentle touch. You are reading of a profound idea, and the crackle of the logs sounds like a quiet applause. The fire becomes the soundtrack to the story. It is the reader’s companion, the silent witness to our inner travels.

In this digital age, we are often told that books are dying, that the physical page is obsolete. But I would argue that the book and the fire share a secret. They are both rebels against the cult of speed. They both require patience. They both reward stillness. They are both a form of defiance against a world that wants everything instantly.

To read by firelight is to reclaim a piece of our humanity. It is to say that some things cannot be rushed. That wisdom is not a download, but a slow burn. That the best stories are not the ones that shout the loudest, but the ones that whisper the longest.

So, my friends, as the nights grow longer, I encourage you to find your own fire—be it a hearth, a campfire, or even a single candle. Find a book that has been waiting for you. And in that quiet, warm space, let the two of them speak to you.

Let the fire warm your bones, and let the book warm your heart. For in that simple, timeless act, we connect not only with the characters on the page, but with every human soul who has ever sought refuge from the dark in the glow of a flame and the promise of a story.

Thank you.

title: Of Gardens
text:
Here is an English essay on gardens, written in a refined and lyrical style.

---

 Of Gardens

There is a profound and quiet magic to a garden. It is not the loud, demanding magic of a storm or the breathtaking spectacle of a mountain range, but something gentler, more intimate—a whispered conversation between humanity and nature. To step into a well-tended garden is to enter a sacred space, a living poem composed of earth, water, and light.

A garden is, in its purest form, a collaboration. Nature provides the raw, untamed soul of the thing: the stubborn persistence of a seed, the intricate architecture of a leaf, the audacious colour of a petal. It offers the soil, rich and dark, and the sun, a generous patron. We, in turn, offer our own humble gifts: a guiding hand, a discerning eye, a willing back. We become temporary curators of a beauty that will long outlive us. Our role is not to command, but to suggest; to prune a branch here, to place a stone there, to create a frame for a view that nature has already painted.

The true essence of a garden, however, is not found in its flawless execution. It resides in its quiet imperfections. It is in the moss that clings to a shaded stone, the way a vine chooses its own erratic path up a wall, the audacity of a weed that appears where it was least expected. These are not flaws to be corrected, but verses in the garden’s own story. They remind us that we are partners in a dance, not masters of a domain. A garden that is too perfect feels sterile, a museum piece. A garden with a little wildness in its heart feels alive, breathing, and real.

To wander through such a place is to engage in a form of meditation. The mind, so often cluttered with the frantic noise of the modern world, begins to quiet. The gentle rustle of leaves becomes a lullaby. The scent of damp earth and blooming jasmine is a balm. The soft, yielding touch of a petal or the rough, enduring feel of bark grounds us in the present moment. A garden does not demand our attention; it simply offers its own. It invites us to slow down, to breathe, to remember the simple rhythm of things that grow not for ambition, but for the sheer, unadulterated joy of being.

And in this act of tending, we cultivate more than just plants. We cultivate patience, observing the slow unfurling of a fern. We cultivate hope, planting a bulb in the autumn and trusting in a spring we cannot yet see. We learn acceptance, understanding that some things will flourish and others will not, and that both are part of the cycle. The garden becomes a mirror, reflecting back to us the seasons of our own lives—our own times of blossoming, of quiet dormancy, and of necessary pruning.

Ultimately, a garden is a testament of faith. It is an act of optimism, a declaration that tomorrow is worth preparing for. It is a promise of renewal, whispered in a language of green and gold, a promise that after every winter, no matter how harsh, the world will, once again, find a way to bloom. And in that promise, we find a peace that is as deep and as enduring as the roots themselves.

title: 老人和他的狗
text:
A Practical Guide for the Elderly and Their Dogs

 Step 1: Choosing the Right Dog
- Consider a breed or size that matches your energy level and living space
- Smaller or senior dogs are often easier to manage
- Look for a calm temperament rather than a high-energy breed
- If possible, adopt from a shelter — staff can help match you with a suitable companion

 Step 2: Preparing Your Home
- Remove tripping hazards such as loose rugs and tangled cords
- Set up a comfortable bed, food and water bowls, and a designated toilet area
- Keep dog supplies in easy-to-reach places to avoid bending or climbing
- Install baby gates if you want to limit your dog to certain rooms

 Step 3: Establishing a Daily Routine
- Feed your dog at the same times each day
- Take short, regular walks — twice a day is usually enough for small dogs
- Schedule toilet breaks consistently, especially in the morning and before bed
- Set aside time each day for petting and bonding

 Step 4: Walking Safely
- Use a comfortable, well-fitted harness or collar and a sturdy leash
- Choose flat, even paths and avoid slippery or uneven ground
- Walk during cooler hours to prevent overheating for both of you
- Bring a bag for waste and a small bottle of water
- If walking is difficult, consider a dog stroller or a fenced yard

 Step 5: Managing Health and Hygiene
- Keep up with vet visits, vaccinations, and flea/tick prevention
- Groom your dog regularly — brush gently and check for skin issues
- Bathe your dog only as needed to avoid drying out its skin
- Keep nails trimmed to prevent scratching and discomfort

 Step 6: Handling Emergencies
- Save your vet's number and the nearest emergency animal clinic
- Keep a basic first-aid kit for both you and your dog
- If you fall or feel unwell while walking, stay calm and call for help
- Consider a medical alert device to wear on walks

 Step 7: Planning for the Unexpected
- Arrange a friend, neighbor, or family member who can help care for your dog
- Write down feeding schedules, medications, and vet information for caregivers
- Consider pet insurance or a savings fund for vet bills
- If hospitalization is possible, identify a temporary foster option in advance

 Step 8: Enjoying the Bond
- Talk to your dog often — it provides comfort and companionship
- Gentle play, brushing, and sitting together are all valuable activities
- Celebrate small moments; the emotional benefits go both ways
- Remember: a dog can greatly reduce loneliness and increase daily purpose

 Quick Checklist
- [ ] Suitable dog chosen
- [ ] Home made safe and dog-friendly
- [ ] Daily routine established
- [ ] Safe walking habits in place
- [ ] Vet and health care up to date
- [ ] Emergency contacts saved
- [ ] Backup care plan arranged

With patience and preparation, an elderly person and their dog can enjoy a safe, happy, and deeply rewarding life together.

title: 唐吉诃德
text:
The Knight of the Mournful Countenance

He rode out at dawn, when the world was still soft with sleep and the wind carried the scent of something ancient—dust, perhaps, or dreams. Don Quixote de la Mancha, thin as a question mark, armored in rust and conviction, tilted at windmills that he alone could see as giants. And in that solitary act of defiance, he became something more than a madman. He became a mirror.

Cervantes gave us a man who read too many books and believed them. But is that not, in some quiet way, what all of us do? We read the world through the lens of our longings. We see giants where others see only windmills. We mistake inns for castles, peasants for princesses, because the heart refuses to live in a world that is merely ordinary.

Sancho Panza, fat with common sense, rides beside him—the eternal counterweight. "Look, señor," he says, "those are not giants, but windmills." But Quixote does not hear. Or perhaps he hears, and chooses otherwise. For what is sanity, in the end, but a collective agreement about what is real? And what is madness but the courage to disagree?

There is something unbearably beautiful about a man who refuses to be disillusioned. Who, when knocked down by the turning blades, rises again, bruised and undeterred, and says: "It was not a windmill. It was a giant in disguise." He will not surrender his vision. He will not let the world tell him what it is.

And so he rides on, through the dusty plains of La Mancha, through the centuries, through the pages of our own lives. We laugh at him, yes. But we also love him. Because in his absurdity, we recognize our own. We too have tilted at things that would not yield. We too have loved people who did not exist as we imagined them. We too have fought battles that no one else could see.

Perhaps that is the secret. Don Quixote is not a warning. He is an invitation. An invitation to live with a little less certainty and a little more hope. To see the world not as it is, but as it might be. To be, in our own small way, knights of the mournful countenance—tired, yes, but still riding. Still believing. Still tilting at whatever windmills stand between us and our dreams.

For in the end, what is life but a long, beautiful delusion? And what is death but the moment we stop believing?

So let us ride. Let us ride with Quixote, into the fading light, into the impossible. Let the windmills turn. Let the world call us mad.

We will not stop.

title: On Walking
text:
On Walking

I confess I am not one of those who walk for the sake of a destination. To be sure, there is a sort of man—and a very estimable sort he is—who sets out with a purpose fixed as firmly as the nails in his boots: to reach the top of a hill, to cross a field, to arrive at some appointed place by the stroke of a certain hour. He marches with his eyes upon the ground, or perhaps upon the horizon, and he counts his steps as a miser counts his coins. But I am not of his company. When I walk, I walk as the clouds walk—without haste, without aim, without any notion of arriving.

The morning is the best time for it. Not the very early morning, when the dew still lies in wait for the hem of your coat, and the lark has but just begun to practise his ascending scale—no, not that; but the hour when the sun has climbed a little above the hedge, and the shadows are still long enough to be companionable. Then the air is cool and sweet, and the grass gives back a fragrance that is half of earth and half of heaven. You step out of your door, and the world is all before you, and you have no more concern for the morrow than the thrush has for the price of wheat.

I love a lane—a proper English lane, with its high banks and its tangled hedges, where the honeysuckle creeps over the hawthorn, and the wild rose peeps out like a shy country girl at a fair. The lane winds and turns, and you never know what may be around the corner: perhaps a field of golden buttercups, perhaps a brook that chatters over the stones as if it had a secret to tell, perhaps a cottage with a garden full of hollyhocks and a cat asleep on the warm flagstones. There is no hurry in a lane. The blackbird knows it, and the snail knows it, and the old man leaning on his gate knows it. They all look at you with a quiet eye, as much as to say, “Why should you hurry? The day is long, and the world is wide.”

And then, if you are lucky, you may come upon a meadow. A meadow is a poem that no poet ever wrote, a symphony that no musician ever scored. It is the earth’s own green hymn of praise, sung in a thousand keys of grass and flower. The cowslips nod their heads in the breeze, and the clover hums with bees, and the little brown butterflies flit from stem to stem as if they were the very thoughts of the meadow made visible. Here you may lie down and look up at the sky, and watch the white clouds sail by like ships on a sea of blue. You may close your eyes and listen to the wind—the wind that has no words, yet tells you all you need to know.

It is a strange thing, but I have often found that I think best when I am not trying to think at all. The mind, like a stream, must be left to find its own channel. When I sit at my desk and summon my thoughts as a general summons his troops, they come slowly and sullenly, and they will not fight. But when I am walking, with no more care than the daisies, the thoughts come unbidden, like friends who drop in at tea-time, and they sit down and talk with me, and I am the better for their company. It is not that I solve my problems on these walks—no, I rather lose them, which is a far greater thing. The problem that seemed so vast in the candle-light dwindles and fades in the sunlight, until at last it is no bigger than a pebble, and I wonder why I ever stumbled over it.

Some men walk to forget, and some to remember; but I walk to be. To be, and to let the world be. To feel the good earth under my feet, and the good air in my lungs, and the good sun on my face. To hear the robin sing his evening song, and to see the first star come out over the darkening hill. These are the simple things, and they are enough. The world is too much with us, as the poet said; but here, in a quiet lane, with the hedges on either side and the sky above, the world is not too much—it is just enough, and no more.

So let the great ones stride along the dusty roads of history, and let the philosophers argue in their cloisters, and let the merchants count their gains. I will take my staff and my old coat, and I will go down the lane, and over the meadow, and up the hill, and I will come home when the moon rises, and I will be content. For I have learned, in my humble way, that the best of life is not to be found in the marketplace, nor in the palace, nor in the crowded street; but in the quiet places, where the grass grows green and the wind blows soft, and a man may walk with God as Adam did in the cool of the day.

And if you ask me why I walk, I will answer you simply: because the path is there, and the day is fair, and my heart is light. Is that not reason enough?

title: 乡间的清晨
text:
The Morning in the Countryside

I have often thought that the true beginning of a day is not to be found in the city. There, the morning is a grudging, mechanical affair—a sudden blaze of electric light, the harsh clangour of alarm bells, the hurried footsteps upon cold pavements. It is a birth without travail, a dawn without mystery. But in the countryside, the morning is a slow and sacred unfolding, a ritual performed in silence and in light.

I remember such a morning, not long ago, when I had taken refuge from the weary world in a small cottage nestled among the hills. I had left the window open, as is my habit, so that the night air might visit me as I slept. And so it was that I was awakened not by any sound of man, but by a gradual brightness that seemed to seep through my very eyelids. The first light of dawn is a timid thing, a pale grey whisper that steals across the sky like a secret. It does not demand attention; it simply arrives, as quietly as a thought.

I rose and went to the window. The world outside was still half-asleep. A thin mist lay over the meadow like a bridal veil, softening every edge and blurring every line. The trees stood motionless, as if they too had just awakened and were reluctant to stir. And then, from somewhere in the distance, came the first sound—the low, gentle lowing of a cow. It was not a noise, but a note, a single cello string plucked in the vast silence. Another followed, and then another, until the whole valley seemed to hum with a quiet music.

I dressed and stepped outside. The grass was wet with dew, and each blade held a tiny globe of light, as if the earth had wept diamonds in the night. The air was cool and clean, carrying the scent of damp earth and wild thyme. I walked down a narrow path that led to a small brook, where the water murmured over smooth stones, telling its ancient story to no one in particular. A robin perched on a low branch, eyeing me with a mixture of curiosity and reproach, as if to say, "You are late. The morning has already begun without you."

And indeed, it had. For as I stood there, the sun began to rise in earnest. It did not burst forth in glory, as it does in paintings, but rather climbed slowly, patiently, as if it had all the time in the world. The mist began to lift, curling upward like incense from a hidden altar. The hills emerged from the grey, first as shadows, then as shapes, and finally as living things—green and gold and brown, waking to the touch of warmth. The birds, which had been silent, now broke into a chorus of praise. Even the brook seemed to sing more brightly.

I thought of the city then, of its artificial dawns and its hurried mornings. How much we lose, I mused, by trading the natural for the convenient. We have conquered the night with our electric lights, but in doing so, we have forgotten the poetry of the dark. We have banished the silence with our engines, but we have also banished the small, precious sounds that silence makes possible. We have, in short, gained the world and lost our souls.

But here, in the countryside, the soul is not lost. It is found anew each morning, in the dew and the mist, in the lowing of cattle and the song of birds, in the slow, deliberate rising of the sun. Here, time is not a tyrant but a friend. Here, one can breathe. Here, one can be.

I returned to the cottage as the morning fully bloomed. The mist was gone, the sky was a clear, tender blue, and the world was busy with its small, essential tasks. A farmer was already in the field, his hoe rising and falling with a rhythm as old as Cain. A woman was hanging laundry on a line, the white sheets flapping like sails in the breeze. Children were running down a lane, their laughter rising like bubbles in the air.

I sat down at the wooden table by the window and poured myself a cup of tea. The steam curled upward, mingling with the sunlight that now streamed through the glass. I thought of the day ahead, with its small duties and quiet pleasures. I thought of the evening, with its long shadows and gentle coolness. And I thought of the next morning, which would come as this one had—not with a shout, but with a whisper; not with violence, but with grace.

For the morning in the countryside is not merely a time of day. It is a state of being. It is a reminder that the world is not ours to command, but ours to receive. It is a gift, freely given, to those who have the patience to wait for it, and the humility to wonder at it.

And so I say to you, if you would know the true meaning of dawn, do not look to the city. Go instead to the country. Rise before the sun. Stand in the silence. And wait. The morning will come to you as it has come to me—not as an event, but as a blessing.

title: 山间小路
text:
Here is a bedtime fairy tale about a mountain path, written in English.

---

The Little Path's Secret

High up in the Misty Mountains, where the clouds liked to play hide-and-seek with the peaks, there was a little path. It wasn't a big, wide road for cars or trucks. It was a small, winding path, just right for a rabbit to hop along or a child to wander.

This little path was very old. It had been there for longer than the oldest pine tree could remember. It was made of soft, packed earth and smooth, grey stones that sparkled when the morning dew kissed them.

The path was a friendly path. It loved the feel of tiny, curious feet. It loved the way the sun made dappled patterns on its back and the way the rain made it smell fresh and new.

One evening, as the sun began to paint the sky in shades of pink and orange, a little girl named Lily came to the path. She was staying in a cabin nearby and couldn't sleep. She sat down at the very beginning of the path, where it started under a big, sleepy oak tree.

"I wonder where you go," Lily whispered to the path.

To her surprise, a soft, rustling voice answered. It sounded like the wind in the leaves. "I go everywhere and nowhere," said the path. "I go to the top of the world and to the secret heart of the forest."

Lily's eyes grew wide. "Can you show me?"

"Not tonight," the path whispered gently. "It's time for all little girls to be in bed. But I can tell you a secret."

Lily leaned in close, her cheek almost touching the cool earth.

"The secret," said the path, "is that I am not just a path. Every stone you see is a wish from a traveler who came before you. The smooth, white one was a wish for a safe journey home from a little rabbit. The sparkly, grey one was a wish for a friend from a lonely fox. And the big, flat one you're sitting on? That was a wish for a beautiful day from a little girl, just like you."

Lily looked down at the stones. They didn't look like ordinary stones anymore. They looked like tiny, sleeping stars.

"What happens to the wishes?" she asked.

"The mountain collects them," the path explained. "It takes all the wishes and turns them into the most beautiful sunrises and the gentlest breezes. So whenever you see a really pretty sunrise, you'll know it's made of happy wishes."

Lily smiled. She felt warm and safe. She gave the path a gentle pat. "Thank you for the secret," she said.

"Goodnight, little one," the path whispered, its voice fading into the sound of the evening crickets. "Follow your dreams. They are the best paths of all."

Lily walked back to her cabin, her heart full of the path's secret. She climbed into bed, and as she closed her eyes, she dreamed of sparkling stones, friendly animals, and a little path that held the wishes of the world.

And the little path, under the light of the moon, felt a new, tiny stone appear. It was a smooth, warm pebble, and it held a wish for sweet dreams.

It was the happiest wish of all.

title: Of Small Things
text:
Here is an argumentative essay on "Of Small Things."

---

 Of Small Things

We live in an age that venerates the colossal. Our headlines celebrate billion-dollar valuations, our screens are filled with superheroes saving entire universes, and our ambitions are often measured in grand, sweeping gestures. We are taught to dream big, to aim for the moon, to make a dent in the universe. In this relentless pursuit of the monumental, we risk overlooking a quieter, yet more profound, truth: the immense power of small things. While grand gestures may capture the imagination, it is the accumulation of small, consistent actions that truly shapes our character, builds our world, and ultimately defines our legacy.

The primary reason for the supremacy of small things is their role in forging character and achieving mastery. We often mistake a single, dramatic event for the source of success or failure, but reality is far more granular. Consider the mastery of a musician. It is not one electrifying performance that makes a virtuoso, but the thousands of hours of solitary, repetitive practice—the daily scales, the tedious drills, the quiet pursuit of perfection in a single chord. Similarly, physical fitness is not the result of one heroic workout, but of the small, daily choices: taking the stairs instead of the elevator, choosing water over soda, a short walk after dinner. These actions are individually insignificant, but compounded over time, they become an unstoppable force. As Aristotle is often credited with saying, "We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act, but a habit." The small things are the very building blocks of our habits, and therefore, of our character.

Furthermore, the small things are the bedrock of our relationships and the fabric of our communities. A grand, expensive gift can be forgotten, but a handwritten note of encouragement can be cherished for a lifetime. The strength of a family is not built on annual, elaborate vacations but on the nightly ritual of sharing a meal, the simple question "How was your day?", and the consistent, small acts of kindness and attention that say, "I see you, and I care." On a societal level, a community is not defined by its magnificent cathedrals or towering skyscrapers, but by the countless small courtesies exchanged between strangers: a held door, a genuine smile, a helping hand for a neighbor. These micro-interactions are the invisible threads that weave the social fabric, creating a sense of belonging and mutual trust that no grand civic project could ever mandate. The erosion of these small civilities is the first sign of a community's decay.

Finally, the philosophy of "small things" offers a powerful antidote to the overwhelming nature of modern life. The grand problems of the world—climate change, poverty, social injustice—are so immense that they can induce a paralyzing sense of helplessness. We feel that our individual contributions are but a drop in the ocean. However, the power of small things reframes the problem. We cannot single-handedly solve climate change, but we can choose to recycle, reduce our consumption, or plant a tree. We cannot eliminate poverty, but we can donate a can of food, volunteer at a local shelter, or mentor a child. These actions matter, not only for their aggregate effect but for their psychological impact. They empower us, transforming us from passive observers into active participants. They remind us that we are not powerless and that a meaningful life is not about waiting for a chance to perform a grand deed, but about recognizing the potential for goodness in every small moment.

In conclusion, the world may shout for grandeur, but wisdom whispers of the small. It is in the consistent, humble, and often unseen actions that we find the true wellspring of character, the enduring bonds of love, and the practical power to effect change. The grand edifice of a life, a relationship, or a society is not built in a day by a single, monumental effort, but brick by brick, moment by moment, through the quiet, cumulative power of small things. To ignore this is to build on sand; to embrace it is to build on stone.

title: 冬日的炉火
text:
Here is a short essay about "冬日的炉火" (The Winter Hearth).

---

 The Winter Hearth

There are few comforts that rival the simple, profound warmth of a hearth fire in winter. It is more than just a source of heat; it is a focal point of the home, a living, breathing heart that beats against the cold, indifferent world outside. As the wind howls and frost etches its intricate patterns on the windowpanes, the hearth becomes a sanctuary.

The fire itself is a hypnotic dance. We watch as the flames, in hues of saffron, amber, and deep crimson, lick at the blackened logs. They are never still, constantly shifting, creating and destroying tiny, glowing cities of embers that rise and fade into the chimney. The wood crackles and sighs, a sound that speaks of time and transformation, while the resinous scent of burning pine or oak fills the air—a perfume of memory and solace.

This warmth draws people together. In its glow, the world shrinks to the size of the room. Conversations become softer, silences more comfortable. It is a place for storytelling, for quiet reflection, for simply being. The hearth is a silent witness to family life, to whispered secrets and booming laughter, to the quiet contentment of a cat curled in a tight ball on the rug. It creates a space where time seems to slow, where the frantic pace of the modern world is held at bay by a wall of gentle heat.

Ultimately, the winter hearth is a symbol of hope and resilience. It is our primal answer to the darkness and the cold. To sit before it is to feel a deep, ancestral sense of peace and security. It is the promise that even in the longest, coldest night, there is a light that endures, a warmth that welcomes, and a place where the spirit can be, for a moment, perfectly at rest.

title: 故乡的河
text:
The River of My Hometown

There are rivers that map a country, and rivers that map a heart. The one that flows through my memory belongs to the latter geography—a modest, unhurried stream that once bisected my childhood like a silver thread stitching two halves of a green quilt. I do not know if it still runs, or if it has been tamed by concrete and made to disappear beneath the ambitions of a town that outgrew it. But in the country of the mind, it is always summer there, and the water is always cold.

I remember it first as a sound before it was a sight. On still nights, with the window open, it entered the house not as a roar but as a murmur—a low, continuous conversation between stones and water, the kind of sound that does not disturb sleep but deepens it. It was the background music of my boyhood, so constant that I only noticed it when it stopped, as when a clock halts and the silence becomes louder than the ticking. That river was the pulse of the place; without it, the town would have been a body without blood.

By day, it was a kingdom of light. The sun, filtering through the willows that leaned over the banks like old men gazing into mirrors, scattered coins of gold upon the surface. Minnows darted in the shallows, quick as thoughts, and the smooth stones underfoot were warm from the morning. We children waded in, our trousers rolled to the knee, searching for the perfect pebble—flat, round, and heavy enough to skip. The river taught us patience. It taught us that some things cannot be rushed, that the best treasures are often buried in silt, and that the current, though gentle, is always stronger than the hand that tries to hold it still.

There were deeper pools, too, where the water turned the color of tea and the reeds stood sentinel. It was there the older boys fished, their lines disappearing into the dark, and it was there I first understood that a river has secrets. It carries away what we give it—a fallen leaf, a whispered wish, a stolen afternoon—and returns them transformed, or not at all. The river was a teacher of impermanence. It showed me that nothing stays, that the water I touched today is not the water I touched yesterday, and yet the river remains.

In the evenings, the women came to wash. They knelt on the flat stones, their arms moving in rhythms older than memory, and their voices rose and fell in gossip and lullaby. The river was their forum, their confessional, their shared kitchen. It belonged to everyone and to no one. It was the one place where the hierarchies of the town dissolved, where the schoolmaster's wife and the farmer's daughter scrubbed the same linen in the same water. The river was democracy in its purest form—cold, clear, and indifferent to the names we give ourselves.

I left the town when I was eighteen, carried away by a different current—the one that pulls the young toward cities and futures. I did not say goodbye to the river. I did not think I needed to. I assumed it would wait, as it always had, patient and unchanging. But rivers, like people, do not wait. They move. They silt up. They are dammed, diverted, forgotten. The town grew. The willows were cut. The washing stones were replaced by machines. And the river, no longer needed, became a drain, then a ditch, then a memory.

Yet in my dreams, it still runs. I hear it on quiet nights, in the space between waking and sleep, and I am ten years old again, barefoot on the warm stones, the water curling around my ankles like a greeting. I have lived by other rivers since—the great, brown, industrial ones that carry barges and pollution and the weight of cities. They are impressive, but they are not mine. They do not know my name. They do not remember the boy who once believed that if he followed the current far enough, he would find the edge of the world.

The river of my hometown was not a grand river. It had no legends, no battles, no poets to sing its praises. It was simply there—a fact of nature, a fact of childhood, a fact of love. And perhaps that is enough. Perhaps the rivers that matter most are not the ones that appear on maps, but the ones that carve their channels through the soft earth of the heart, leaving behind a bed that never quite dries.

I do not know if I will ever return. The town I knew is gone, and the river, if it survives, is not the river I remember. But that is the nature of memory—it preserves what time destroys. And so I keep my river where it cannot be dammed, where it cannot be polluted, where it runs clear and cold and eternal. It is the river of my hometown, and it flows through me still, a quiet current under the noise of the world, reminding me of who I was, and of the simple, sacred places that made me.

In the end, we are all rivers. We begin in the hills, we gather strength, we carve our paths through the plains of our lives, and we empty into something larger than ourselves. And if we are lucky, someone remembers the sound of our water, long after we have gone.

title: 雨后的村庄
text:
The rain had stopped. In the village, everything was dripping and glistening. The smell of wet earth and woodsmoke filled the air, a scent that was both ancient and new. The storm had been a fierce one, a tantrum of wind and water that had lashed the cottages and bent the ancient willow by the stream. Now, a profound quiet reigned, broken only by the rhythmic *plink-plink-plink* of water dripping from the eaves into a wooden bucket.

Elias stepped out of his small stone house and took a deep breath. The air was so clean it felt like a drink of cold spring water. The dirt path, usually a dusty ribbon, was now a small, muddy river, carving channels through the village. He pulled his worn leather boots on, the soles sinking slightly into the soft ground.

He walked towards the center of the village, where the old stone well stood. The world around him was a masterpiece of post-storm detail. Each leaf on the great oak tree held a perfect, shimmering droplet. A spider's web, once invisible, was now a necklace of diamonds, strung between two fence posts. The thatched roofs of the cottages, dark and heavy with moisture, seemed to breathe, releasing a fine mist into the cool air.

Children were the first to break the silence. They burst from their homes, laughing and shouting, their bare feet splashing in the puddles. They launched twig boats into the new streams that ran along the roadside, their voices high and clear. Old Man Hemlock, who had lived in the village for eighty years, sat on his porch, watching them with a gentle smile. He didn't need to say anything. His presence, like the rain, was a part of the village's rhythm.

Elias reached the well and drew up a bucket of water. It was cold and sweet. He drank deeply, feeling it wash away the last vestiges of sleep. He looked around. The vegetable gardens were vibrant, the greens of the lettuce and the reds of the radishes almost impossibly bright. The world had been washed clean.

A single bird began to sing, its notes hesitant at first, then gaining confidence. Another joined in, and soon the air was filled with a chorus of chirps and trills. The village was waking up, not to the harsh alarm of a clock, but to the gentle summons of a world renewed.

Elias smiled. The storm had been a disruption, a reminder of nature's power. But the aftermath, this quiet, glistening peace, was its gift. It was a time for reflection, for connection, for the simple joy of being alive in a world that had, once again, been made new. He sat on the edge of the well, watching the children play, listening to the birds, and feeling, for the first time in a long time, a deep and abiding sense of peace. The village, like the earth, had been refreshed. And so had he.

title: 收割的季节
text:
Here is a speech in English about the harvest season:

---

The Season of Harvest

Good morning, everyone.

There is a moment every year that arrives not with a trumpet blast, but with a quiet golden glow. The air turns crisp. The fields, once green and waving, now stand heavy with grain. The orchards bend low under the weight of their fruit. And we know — without needing a calendar to tell us — that the season of harvest has come.

The harvest season is one of humanity's oldest and most universal experiences. Long before we had cities or machines or written words, our ancestors looked to the fields and understood a simple truth: what you plant with patience, you reap with gratitude.

But the harvest is about more than crops. It is a metaphor for everything we cultivate in our lives.

Think about a farmer. In the spring, they sow seeds that look like nothing more than tiny, dry specks. They water them. They wait. They protect the young shoots from frost and pests. Day after day, they show up — not because they see immediate results, but because they trust the process. And then, months later, the harvest arrives. Not suddenly, but inevitably.

That is the rhythm of every worthwhile endeavor. The student who studies late into the night. The artist who practices when no one is watching. The parent who teaches a child right from wrong. The worker who builds something with care. None of them see the harvest on the day they plant. But the harvest comes — for those who do not give up.

The harvest season also teaches us about community. In traditional farming cultures, the harvest was never a solitary task. Neighbors came together. Families worked side by side. The whole village celebrated. Why? Because no one person could bring in the harvest alone. And no one person should enjoy it alone, either.

In our modern lives, we sometimes forget this. We chase individual success. We measure our worth by personal achievement. But the truth is, we are all part of a larger field. Our harvests — our joys, our accomplishments, our moments of abundance — are meant to be shared.

There is another lesson the harvest teaches us: gratitude. When the barns are full and the tables are set, we remember that not every season is a harvest season. There are years of drought. There are years of storm. There are years when the seeds we plant do not grow. And so, when the harvest does come, we give thanks — not just for the abundance, but for the resilience that carried us through the lean times.

So today, as we gather in this season of harvest, let us ask ourselves: What have we planted? What are we nurturing? And what are we ready to reap?

Let us be patient with our seeds. Let us be generous with our harvest. And let us always remember that the season of harvest is not just about what we gather — it is about who we become in the process.

Thank you.

title: On Idleness
text:
On Idleness

There is a species of idleness that the world hath ever been too ready to condemn, confounding it, in its hasty judgment, with mere sloth and the drowsy vice of unwrought hours. Yet I hold that there liveth a gentler idleness, born not of indolence but of contemplation, whose proper seat is the green meadow and the shaded lane, and whose voice is the low murmur of bees among the clover.

To lie upon a bank in June, when the sun is tempered by a wandering cloud, and to watch the shadows travel over the face of the hill as though the earth herself were dreaming—this is no waste of time, but a kind of prayer that the tongue knoweth not how to utter. The brook goeth by with its endless and indifferent song, and the willow bendeth over it, and a dragon-fly hangeth in the air like a jewel loosened from its setting. What hast thou to do with the world's business in such an hour? Let the merchant count his gains, and the statesman plot his factions; the meadow is thine, and the silence, and the slow procession of the summer day.

I have observed that men are ashamed of leisure, as though it were a garment out of fashion. They must be ever doing, ever striving, as if the universe would fall should their hands be stilled. But the universe, methinks, is better served by him who hath learned to be still and to look upon it with a quiet eye. The stars keep their courses without haste; the seasons return without anxiety. Shall man alone be feverish, and call his fever virtue?

There is, moreover, a music in idleness which no labour can produce. The shepherd's pipe, the distant bell of some village church, the rustle of leaves when the wind walketh softly among them—these are the true anthems of the earth, and they are heard only by the idle. The busy man heareth nothing but the clatter of his own affairs, and the world to him is but a market-place.

Let me then, in the evening of my days, choose rather the idle path. Let me sit by the hedge where the wild roses blow, and let the hours pass as they will. For I have learned that Time is not a coin to be spent, but a river upon whose bosom we may lie, and be carried gently, and ask no whither.

title: 月光下的湖
text:
The Lake in Moonlight: A Literary Appreciation

 Abstract

The image of a lake under moonlight constitutes one of the most enduring and evocative motifs in world literature, functioning across cultures and centuries as a site of reflection, transcendence, and existential reckoning. This essay offers a literary appreciation of the moonlight-lake motif through comparative readings of three representative works: William Wordsworth's "Lines Composed a Few Miles above Tintern Abbey" (1798), Li Bai's "Drinking Alone under the Moon" (月下独酌, c. 744), and Henry David Thoreau's *Walden* (1854). Drawing on phenomenological aesthetics and ecocritical theory, the essay argues that the moonlit lake operates as a liminal space in which the boundaries between self and world, presence and absence, and the mundane and the sublime are productively dissolved. Rather than merely a decorative backdrop, the lake in moonlight becomes a narrative and philosophical agent in its own right—a mirror that reflects not only the physical moon but also the interior landscapes of those who behold it.

 1. Introduction

Few natural scenes have exercised so persistent a hold on the literary imagination as a body of water illuminated by moonlight. From the Psalms of the Hebrew Bible to the Tang dynasty poets, from Romanticism to modernism, the moonlit lake recurs as a threshold image—simultaneously still and shifting, familiar and strange. Its appeal lies precisely in its ambiguity: water reflects, but imperfectly; moonlight clarifies, yet also obscures. This essay examines how three very different literary traditions exploit this ambiguity to explore questions of solitude, memory, and belonging.

 2. The Lake as Mirror of the Self: Wordsworth

In Wordsworth's "Tintern Abbey," the speaker recalls how "the sounding cataract / Haunted me like a passion" and how, in later years, he has learned to hear "the still, sad music of humanity" in natural scenes. Although the poem does not center on a lake per se, its climactic meditation on the River Wye exemplifies the Romantic tendency to treat reflective water as a medium of self-knowledge. The moonlit lake in Wordsworth's broader oeuvre—most famously in the "spots of time" passage of *The Prelude*—becomes a screen onto which the poet projects his own moral and imaginative development. The water does not merely reflect the moon; it reflects the observer's changing relationship to nature.

 3. The Lake as Companion in Solitude: Li Bai

Li Bai's "Drinking Alone under the Moon" stages a scene of radical solitude transformed into conviviality:

> *A cup of wine, under the flowering trees;*
> *I drink alone, for no friend is near.*
> *Raising my cup, I beckon the bright moon,*
> *For her, with my shadow, will make three men.*

Here the moonlit setting is not a mirror of the self but a substitute for human society. The lake (or, in some readings, the river) and the moon become imagined companions, dissolving the boundary between solitude and communion. Where Wordsworth's lake interiorizes, Li Bai's exteriorizes—projecting the self outward into a playful, almost theatrical relationship with the natural world.

 4. The Lake as Ethical Teacher: Thoreau

Thoreau's *Walden* opens with a chapter titled "Economy" but quickly turns to "Where I Lived, and What I Lived For," in which the pond becomes a moral and spiritual teacher. In the chapter "The Ponds," Thoreau describes Walden Pond by moonlight as "a perfect forest mirror"—a phrase that captures both its aesthetic purity and its ethical demand. For Thoreau, the moonlit lake is not a site of escape but of confrontation: it asks the observer to simplify, to attend, to live deliberately. The lake's stillness becomes a rebuke to the "quiet desperation" of ordinary life.

 5. Conclusion

Across these three traditions, the lake in moonlight emerges as a liminal figure—neither purely natural nor purely symbolic, neither wholly self nor wholly other. It is a mirror that reflects the observer's own longings, a companion that consoles solitude, and a teacher that demands ethical attention. To read the moonlit lake is thus to read the human condition in its most reflective and vulnerable mode. The motif endures not because it offers answers, but because it stages, with unusual clarity, the questions we cannot stop asking.

 References

Li, Bai. "Drinking Alone under the Moon." *The Columbia Book of Chinese Poetry: From Early Times to the Thirteenth Century*, translated by Burton Watson, Columbia University Press, 1984, pp. 210–211.

Thoreau, Henry David. *Walden; or, Life in the Woods*. 1854. Dover Publications, 1995.

Wordsworth, William. "Lines Composed a Few Miles above Tintern Abbey." 1798. *The Norton Anthology of English Literature*, edited by Stephen Greenblatt, 10th ed., vol. D, W. W. Norton, 2018, pp. 288–292.

Wordsworth, William. *The Prelude: 1799, 1805, 1850*. Edited by Jonathan Wordsworth et al., W. W. Norton, 1979.

Bachelard, Gaston. *Water and Dreams: An Essay on the Imagination of Matter*. 1942. Translated by Edith R. Farrell, Dallas Institute of Humanities and Culture, 1983.

Buell, Lawrence. *The Environmental Imagination: Thoreau, Nature Writing, and the Formation of American Culture*. Harvard University Press, 1995.

title: On the Passing of Time
text:
Here is a reading response to *On the Passing of Time*.

---

 A Review of *On the Passing of Time*

*On the Passing of Time* is not merely a book; it is an experience, a profound meditation on the most elusive and democratic force in our lives. Reading it feels less like consuming information and more like sitting quietly by a river, watching the current carry leaves, twigs, and memories downstream. The book doesn’t attempt to solve the mystery of time but instead invites the reader to feel its texture, to acknowledge its relentless power, and ultimately, to find a fragile peace within its flow.

The central theme, as the title suggests, is the ephemeral nature of existence. The author masterfully illustrates that time is not a static concept to be studied but a dynamic, living phenomenon we are all immersed in. Through a tapestry of poignant anecdotes, philosophical reflections, and scientific insights, the book paints a vivid picture of time as both a creator and a destroyer. It is the force that allows a child to grow, a love to blossom, and a civilization to rise. Yet, it is also the same force that brings wrinkles to a face, fades a cherished memory, and turns empires to dust. This duality is the book's beating heart.

What makes *On the Passing of Time* so impactful is its refusal to offer easy comfort. It does not pretend that loss is not loss or that the fleeting nature of joy does not make it bittersweet. Instead, it argues that the value of a moment is intrinsically linked to its impermanence. A sunset is beautiful *because* it is temporary. A laugh is precious *because* it cannot be held forever. This perspective is both terrifying and liberating. It forces us to confront the anxiety of our own mortality but also compels us to cherish the "now" with a fierce and urgent tenderness.

The book's prose is lyrical and contemplative, with a quiet power that lingers long after the final page is turned. It doesn't shout its wisdom; it whispers it. One of the most resonant passages compares our lives to a single, fleeting note in a grand, cosmic symphony. We may not be the entire song, but the music would be incomplete without us. This idea provides a sense of purpose not in permanence, but in participation. Our significance lies not in lasting forever, but in contributing our unique sound to the chorus of existence while we are here.

In conclusion, *On the Passing of Time* is a powerful and necessary read for anyone who has ever felt the pang of a moment slipping away. It is a book that doesn't just make you think; it makes you feel. It encourages a shift in perspective—from fighting the current of time to learning how to navigate it with grace and awareness. It teaches us that while we cannot stop the clock, we can choose how we fill the hours. We are left not with a sense of despair, but with a quiet resolve to live more fully, love more deeply, and appreciate the fleeting, beautiful gift of our own time.

title: Of Rivers and Memory
text:
Of Rivers and Memory

There is a river that runs through the country of my childhood, and though I have not seen it in thirty years, I can yet hear it plainly on certain quiet evenings, when the wind falls and the light grows long and gold. It is not a great river as rivers are reckoned in atlases—no Mississippi, no Danube, no Ganges bearing the prayers of millions—but it was great enough for a boy, which is to say it was infinite, and it was mine.

I have come to believe that memory works less like a ledger than like a watershed. We imagine our pasts as straight lines, a chronology of days, but this is the fancy of historians. In truth the mind keeps its records the way the hills keep the rain: everything that falls upon the high ground eventually finds the same valley, and the smallest brook is cousin to the widest flood. A scent of cut grass, a certain slant of autumn light, the sound of water over stones—these are tributaries, and they run together in us until the particular and the universal are no longer to be told apart.

Consider how a river remembers. It does not, as we do, keep a single channel and call that the truth. It meanders; it cuts new banks and abandons old ones; it leaves oxbows standing in the meadows like questions no longer asked. The geologist tells us that the river's memory is written in the land itself—in the gravel beds, the terraces, the rich black silt that feeds the corn. And so it is with us. The past is not behind us; it is beneath us, a sediment on which we stand, and we are always, whether we know it or not, building our houses on the floodplain of our own remembering.

I return in thought to that river of my boyhood as a man returns to a shrine—not to worship, exactly, but to be reminded of what he was before he learned to be careful. There was a pool below the milldam where the water ran deep and green, and in summer the minnows hung in it like flecks of light made solid. I remember the cold shock of it on a July morning, the way the current tugged at my ankles with a gentle insistence, as though it had somewhere to be and wished to take me along. I remember the smell of it—that green, mineral breath of wet stone and living water—which no perfumer has ever bottled and no poet, try as he might, has ever quite set down.

And I remember the heron. He stood at the shallows each morning like a gray sentinel, patient as stone, and when he lifted his wings the whole sky seemed to move in them. I have seen herons since, in other waters, and each time I feel the old pull of that first river, and I understand that I am not looking at a bird but at a door, and behind the door a boy is standing, squinting into the sun.

The philosophers tell us that we cannot step twice into the same river, and they are right, but they have told only half the truth. We cannot step twice into the same river, nor can the river ever step twice around the same stone. Yet the river is still the river. It carries the same name, the same water, the same long conversation with the sea. And we are still ourselves, though every cell has been replaced and every belief revised and every love either deepened or grieved. There is a continuity that is not sameness, a persistence that is not stagnation. The river teaches us this if we will sit still long enough to learn it.

What, then, shall we make of memory? Not a museum, I think—not a dim hall of labeled relics behind glass. Memory is better understood as a living watercourse, fed by springs we did not dig and cannot wholly trace. It shapes the land it passes through. It carries the leaves of many autumns. It cuts its banks and changes its course, and sometimes it floods, and sometimes it runs low, and always it moves toward the sea.

I have lived long enough now to have lost the river to the changes of the world—the mill torn down, the dam breached, the banks built up with houses of a newer fashion. But I have not lost the river to memory, for memory is not a place where things are lost. It is a place where things are kept, the way the earth keeps rain long after the clouds have passed—in the roots of trees, in the deep aquifers, in the slow green rising of the spring.

And so I find that I am not, as I once feared, a man estranged from his own beginning. I am a tributary of that river still. It runs in me, as it ran before me, and will run, I trust, in those who come after, long after my name is silt. The water goes down to the sea, and the rain comes up from the sea, and the hills gather the rain, and the river carries it home again. This is the oldest story, and the truest: that nothing is ever truly gone, only gathered, and gathered, and given back.

I sit by the window as the evening deepens, and I hear it—faint, persistent, patient as the stars—the sound of water over stones. It is the river of my childhood, and it is every river, and it is the river of time itself. It asks nothing of me but attention. And I give it, gladly, as a man gives thanks at the end of a long day, knowing that he has been carried all along, and will be carried still, and that the water, though it never rests, never lets him go.

title: 林间的鸟鸣
text:
Here is a reading reflection in English on *Bird Songs in the Woods* (《林间的鸟鸣》).

---

Reflection on *Bird Songs in the Woods*

*Bird Songs in the Woods* is a quiet, luminous piece of writing that invites the reader to slow down and listen. At its heart, the essay (or book) is not really about birds at all—it is about attention, solitude, and the forgotten art of being present in nature.

What struck me most was the author's gentle insistence that the forest is never silent. To an untrained ear, the woods may seem still, but once you truly listen, you discover a whole world of sound: the fluting of a thrush at dawn, the insistent tapping of a woodpecker, the soft rustle of wings among the leaves. The birds do not perform for us; they simply live, and their songs are byproducts of territory, courtship, and joy. The author's prose mirrors this—unhurried, unadorned, yet full of quiet wonder.

There is also a melancholy undertone. As the narrator returns to the woods across seasons, we sense that both the forest and the self are changing. Some birds return; others do not. The songs that once filled a particular grove may fade into memory. This gives the writing a bittersweet beauty—a reminder that listening is also a form of holding on, and that every song is, in its own way, ephemeral.

Reading this work made me realize how rarely I truly listen. In a world saturated with noise—notifications, traffic, endless chatter—the birds offer an alternative: a call to be still, to breathe, and to let the natural world speak first. I found myself closing the book and stepping outside, straining to hear even a single sparrow. And when I finally did, it felt like a gift.

*Bird Songs in the Woods* is not a loud book. It does not argue or persuade. It simply opens a window and says, *Listen.* And if we do, we may hear not only the birds, but also something in ourselves that has been waiting to be heard.

title: Of Rain and Quiet
text:
Here is an English prose piece titled Of Rain and Quiet.

---

 Of Rain and Quiet

There is a kind of hush that only rain can bring.

It does not arrive all at once, but softly, like a memory returning. First, the air changes — a coolness slips through the window, carrying the scent of wet earth and distant clouds. Then comes the sound: a whisper at first, barely there, as if the sky were turning the pages of an old book. And then, gently, the rain begins in earnest, and the world seems to exhale.

I have always loved these hours. The ones where the light fades to a silver-grey, where the trees bow their heads as if in prayer, and where the streets grow quiet, washed clean of hurry. Rain does not ask for attention. It simply falls — on rooftops, on leaves, on the shoulders of strangers — and in doing so, it softens everything it touches.

And with the rain comes the quiet. Not emptiness, but a fullness — a stillness that settles into the bones. The mind, so often restless, grows calm. Thoughts that once clamored for answers now drift like droplets down a windowpane, slow and unhurried. There is no need to speak. There is no need to move. There is only the rain, and the quiet, and the gentle art of simply being.

I think we are all a little more honest in the rain. The masks we wear — of confidence, of busyness, of having everything figured out — grow heavy and slip away. What remains is something softer, something truer. A ache we had forgotten. A hope we had buried. A love we had not dared to name. Rain has a way of washing away the noise until only the heart is left, speaking in its own quiet language.

Perhaps that is why I find comfort here. In a world that never stops shouting, the rain does not compete. It does not demand. It simply is — and in its presence, I remember how to be, too.

So let it fall. Let the clouds empty themselves upon the earth, and let the quiet come. For in the rain, I have found a friend. And in the quiet, I have found myself.
